food.text: Several notable cookbooks were written in southern India in the medieval period, including Lokopakara in 1025 CE and Manasollasa in 1130 CE. They contain both vegetarian and non-vegetarian dishes, which shows how much thought went into cooking in this era.

During the Middle Ages, before the Age of Discovery, the kingdom of Calicut on the Malabar Coast was the centre of Indian pepper exports to the Red Sea and Europe. Black pepper is native to the Malabar Coast, and Arab traders were particularly active in the trade.

In medieval Deccan cuisine, banquets were common among the aristocracy. Multiple courses were served in Dastarkhan style, placed on a long cloth laid on the floor. Food was generally eaten without utensils, by nobility and ordinary people alike.

The Deccan's cuisine was largely local and traditional until the days of the Vijayanagara Empire. When Muhammad bin Tughluq moved his capital from Delhi to Daulatabad, the region was exposed to dishes from other areas and adopted them.

Turkish cuisine began to influence the Deccan in the 14th century, when the Bahmani Sultanate was formed and Turkish nobles were appointed to high positions in the government. The haute cuisine of Hyderabad began to develop after the Bahmani Sultanate was founded.

Cookery writer Pratibha Karan states that biryani is of Indian origin, derived from pilau, which Muslim traders and invaders brought with them. She speculates that pilau was an army dish in medieval India, where armies would prepare a one-pot dish of rice with any available red meat. Over time, different cooking methods turned it into biryani.

Medieval Deccan cooking changed in several ways: dishes based on meat became more common and the use of spices increased. Fresh fruit became a common dessert, and a drink called Kahwa became a popular digestive. Many items were preserved as pickles.
The origin of biryani is debated. It may have been brought to South India before the Mughal era, or pilau may have come to India first, with biryani developed from it before the Mughals adopted it.

Food historian K. T. Achaya first argued that pilau was of older usage in India than biryani, pointing to ancient and early medieval texts like the Mahabharata that described rice cooked with meat. He later conceded that, despite the similar names, those dishes were not the same as the medieval pulao.

art.text: The Cholas used the wealth of their conquests to build long-lasting stone temples and exquisite bronze sculptures. Their imperial period, roughly 850 to 1250 CE, was an age of continuous improvement and refinement in art and architecture.

The Shah Mir sultans of Kashmir blended Persian and local Buddhist building traditions. Sikandar Shah Mir built the Jamia Masjid in Srinagar, a large wooden mosque that incorporates elements of Buddhist pagoda structure.

Islamic patrons needed mosques and tombs, buildings very different from earlier Indian ones. Both were often topped by large domes and used many arches, features hardly used in Hindu temples. They also completely avoided the figurative sculpture that was so important to Hindu temple architecture.

The Eastern Ganga king Narasimhadeva I, who ruled from 1238 to 1264 CE, built the Konark Sun Temple in Odisha. It is now a World Heritage Site. The dynasty prospered through trade and commerce, and its wealth was mostly used in the construction of temples.

Rajaraja I built the Siva temple of Thanjavur in 1009, called the largest and tallest of all Indian temples of its time. It is described as the apex of South Indian architecture. It stands as a memorial to the achievements of the Chola emperors.

Chola craftsmen made lost wax bronzes, many cast as heavy images to be carried in processions on poles. They include the iconic form of Shiva as Nataraja, whose right foot tramples the dwarf Apasmara, who represents ignorance. In recent times many of these priceless Chola bronzes have been stolen from their temples or museums and smuggled out of India into the private collections of art collectors. Chola bronzes are also held in museums including the British Museum and the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York.

Anantavarma Chodaganga Deva, who reigned from 1078 to 1147 CE, founded the Eastern Ganga dynasty. He was a patron of art and literature and is credited with building the famous Jagannath Temple of Puri in Odisha.

Around 1030 the Cholas completed the Brihadisvara Temple at Gangaikonda Cholapuram. Later Chola kings built the Airavatesvara Temple at Darasuram around 1160 and the Kampahareswarar Siva Temple at Tribhuvanam around 1200. All four temples were built over nearly 200 years.

The tomb of Shah Rukn-e-Alam in Multan was built between 1320 and 1324. It is a large octagonal brick mausoleum with polychrome glazed decoration, closer to the styles of Iran and Afghanistan. It was the earliest major monument of the Tughlaq dynasty and was built for a Sufi saint rather than a sultan.

The Adinatha temple at Golakot, a Jain site in Madhya Pradesh, has an elongated shrine room preceded by an open pillared porch. Its layout resembles contemporary mosque architecture. The image chamber contains seventeen large Jina representations.

Two 14th-century wooden mosques in Gilgit-Baltistan, the Chaqchan Mosque in Khaplu, built in 1370, and the Amburiq Mosque in Shigar, have stone-built cores. Their exteriors have elaborately carved wooden galleries, on two levels at Amburiq, adapting traditional local styles.

Few Indian miniatures survive from before about 1000 CE. Those that survive are initially illustrations for Buddhist texts, followed later by Jain and Hindu equivalents. The decline of Buddhism and the vulnerable palm-leaf manuscript support probably explain the rarity of early examples.

war.text: In 1192 the Ghurid forces of Muhammad Ghuri defeated the Rajput Confederacy of Prithviraj Chauhan near Tarain, 110 kilometres north of Delhi. Ghuri tricked Prithviraj with talk of peace, then attacked the Chahamana army before sunrise while it slept after a night of merry-making, and its troops fled in panic. Prithviraj was captured and later killed for treason, and the battle is regarded as a watershed that destroyed Rajput powers for a while and laid the foundation of Muslim rule in North India, which led to the Delhi Sultanate.

The Ghaznavid campaigns in India were a series of military expeditions lasting over two centuries, led notably by Sultan Mahmud of Ghazni (r. 998-1030). Their primary objectives were the acquisition of wealth, the propagation of Islam, and the establishment of Ghaznavid rule in the region. The campaigns included plundering and devastation: at Mathura Mahmud plundered the city and left it in ruins, and at Somnath in 1026 the Ghaznavids looted the temple and destroyed its idols, with 50,000 casualties among the defenders. Conflicts continued until the fall of the Ghaznavids in the late 12th century.

The Eastern Ganga rulers defended their kingdom from constant attacks by Muslim rulers, and were perhaps one of the few empires to have successfully invaded and defeated their Muslim adversaries. King Narasimha Deva I invaded the Muslim kingdom of Bengal and handed a heavy defeat to the Sultan. His military exploits still survive as folklore in Odisha.

Muhammad of Ghor's invasions of India lasted 31 years, from 1175 to 1206. Along the way he extirpated several local dynasties, including the Isma'ilis of Multan, the Ghaznavids of Lahore, the Chauhans of Ajmer, the Tomaras of Delhi and the Jadauns of Bayana. The Ghaznavid ruler Khusrau Malik was brought out of his castle under negotiations, treacherously imprisoned, and later executed along with all of his family. Muhammad himself was assassinated near the Indus on 15 March 1206, and the Ghurid empire fell apart in 1215.

The First Battle of Tarain was fought on 14 January 1191 between the Ghurids under Muhammad of Ghor and the Rajput Confederacy under Prithviraj Chauhan. The Ghurid cavalry opened with arrows, but the Chahamana forces counter-attacked from three sides and dominated the battle. Muhammad of Ghor charged Govind Rai and hit him in the mouth with a lance, breaking two of his teeth. Govind Rai struck back with a javelin and severely wounded Muhammad of Ghor's upper arm. According to Minhaj, Muhammad would have died or been captured had a young soldier not led his horse to safety. The wound was so painful that he could no longer stay on horseback, and the disheartened Ghurid army was routed. The Rajputs won, and Muhammad of Ghor escaped and returned to Ghazni.

The Eastern Ganga king Narasimha Deva I invaded the Muslim kingdom of Bengal and handed a heavy defeat to the Sultan. This ensured the Sultanate never encroached upon Ganga domains for nearly a century. His military exploits still survive today as folklore in Odisha.

The writer Firishta claimed the Chauhan army at the Second Battle of Tarain had 3,000 elephants and 300,000 cavalry and infantry. Modern historians consider this an exaggeration. Kaushik Roy notes that Muslim chroniclers regularly exaggerated Hindu military strength to glorify Muslim kings, and 300,000 was probably the theoretical number all the Rajput kingdoms could mobilize.

After the Ghurid defeat at the First Battle of Tarain, a garrison of 2,000 soldiers under Zia ud-Din Tulaki was left to hold the fort of Tabarhind. It kept the Rajput army at bay for thirteen months. In that time Muhammad of Ghor raised a stronger army of 120,000 men and invaded again.

At the first Tarain battle, the outnumbered Ghurid forces were completely routed, and Muhammad of Ghor was himself wounded in personal combat with Govind Rai of Delhi. He was carried away from the battlefield by a Khalji stripling. The Rajputs did not chase the retreating Ghurids and instead besieged the fort of Tabarhind, which fell after a siege of thirteen months.

In 1034 Ahmad Niyaltigin, a Ghaznavid governor of the Punjab, led campaigns against Indian chieftains and compelled the Thakurs to pay tribute. He crossed the Ganges, travelled along its left bank, and reached Banaras, part of the Kalachuri king Gangeyadeva's realm. There he plundered the markets and returned to Punjab with a substantial haul of gold, silver, and jewels.

After Mas'ud III succeeded Ibrahim as Ghaznavid sultan in 1099, his officer Hajib Tughatigin crossed the Ganges and carried on conquest in India. The king of Kannauj, probably Madanapala, was captured by the Sultan's army and held in captivity. Madanapala's son Govindachandra then defeated the Ghaznavids and released his father from captivity.

In 1196 Muhammad of Ghor captured Bayana from the Jadaun Rajputs after a brief siege, to guard the southern flank of Delhi. He placed it under his senior slave Bahauddin Turghil. Bahauddin then laid siege to Gwalior fort and annexed it after subjugating the Parihar ruler. Earlier, after the second battle of Tarain, the Ghurids had sacked Ajmer, massacring several civilians, taking many as slaves and destroying several Hindu temples; Prithviraj Chauhan, defeated at Tarain, was captured and summarily executed.

Grants by the Gahadavala rulers Chandradeva, Madanapala, Govindachandra and Vijayachandra mention a tax called the Turushkadanda. It was likely used to counter or appease the Ghaznavids. This shows that the Rajput kings recognized the threat of the late 11th century raids, even though the raids were not highly impactful.

literature.text: The Vachana Sahitya tradition of the 12th century is described as purely native and unique in world literature. It arose in Kannada literature, where other works of the medieval period were based on Jain and Hindu principles.

Baba Farid (1173–1266) is often considered the first major Punjabi poet. His Sufi poetry was compiled after his death in the Adi Granth. Some say the high level of Punjabi poetry by Baba Farid, Guru Nanak and Bhai Gurdas suggests Punjabi literature may have evolved much earlier, perhaps in the 9th or 10th centuries.

The Sanskrit Ramayana was retold in several regional languages. Kamban's Tamil version dates to the 12th century and Kirttivas' Bengali version to the 15th century. Gona Budda Reddy's Telugu Ranganath Ramayanamu also belongs to this sequence of vernacular translations.

Sanskrit short poems survive mainly through anthologies. One widely celebrated example is the Subhāṣitaratnakoṣa, or Anthology of Well Said Jewels, compiled by the Buddhist monk Vidyakara (c. 1050–1130). Another, Sridharadasa's Saduktikarṇāmṛta, followed in 1205.

In the 14th century Madhav Kandali rendered the Ramayana as the Saptakanda Ramayana. It is considered the first rendition of the Ramayana into an Indo-Aryan language in the Indian subcontinent. It came after Kamban's Tamil version and before Kirttivas' Bengali one.
Chandidas, who lived in Birbhum in the late 14th century, was among the earliest poets in the Middle Bengali language. Many of his poems deal with the Radha-Krishna theme.

In 1474 Maladhar Basu translated the 10th and 11th cantos of the Sanskrit Srimad Bhagavatam into the Bengali poem Shri Krishna Bijay. It relates the legends of Krishna as a child and is the oldest Bengali narrative poem of the Krishna legend.

Mangal kavyas are Bengali religious texts composed more or less between the 13th and 18th centuries. Written in verse, they usually tell of indigenous deities of rural Bengal, each blended with a Vedic or Hindu mythological god.
Later Sanskrit Hindu texts include works on Hatha Yoga. Among them are the Dattātreyayogaśāstra and the Gorakṣaśataka, both from the 13th century, and the Haṭhayogapradīpikā from the 15th century.

Maladhar Basu was honoured by Rukunuddin Barbak Shah with the title Gunaraj Khan. Neither he nor Chandidas was a Vaishnava, yet both laid the foundation for much of the Vaishnava poetry that followed in Bengal.

science.text: Madhava of Sangamagrama (c. 1340 – 1425) and his Kerala school of astronomy and mathematics were the first to use infinite series approximations for a range of trigonometric functions. They also took decisive steps in analysis.
science.source_title: History of science and technology on the Indian subcontinent

science.text: The origins of the spinning wheel are unclear, but South Asia is one of the probable places it came from. The device certainly reached Europe from India by the 14th century.
science.source_title: History of science and technology on the Indian subcontinent

science.text: Gunpowder and gunpowder weapons were transmitted to India through the Mongol invasions of India. The Mongols were defeated by Alauddin Khalji of the Delhi Sultanate, and some Mongol soldiers remained in northern India after converting to Islam.
science.source_title: History of science and technology on the Indian subcontinent

science.text: Madhava of Sangamagrama, who lived from about 1340 to 1425, is credited with stating the infinite series for π. This was part of the wider work of the Kerala school of astronomy and mathematics.
science.source_title: History of science and technology on the Indian subcontinent

science.text: Gunpowder warfare became common in the region, with events such as the siege of Belgaum in 1473 CE by the Sultan Muhammad Shah Bahmani. Firearms known as top-o-tufak had already existed in the Vijayanagara Empire by 1366 CE.
science.source_title: History of science and technology on the Indian subcontinent

science.text: As part of an embassy to India by the Timurid leader Shah Rukh (1405–1447), 'Abd al-Razzaq mentioned naphtha-throwers mounted on elephants. He also described a variety of pyrotechnics put on display.
science.source_title: History of science and technology on the Indian subcontinent

politics.text: In the early medieval period, the Indian subcontinent held more than 40 different states, hosting a variety of cultures, languages, writing systems, and religions. Some historians place the end of the medieval period in 1526, with the start of the Mughal Empire.

The Delhi Sultanate was established in 1206 by Central Asian Turks and ruled much of northern India in the 14th century. Its decline in the late 14th century followed the invasions of Timur. After the sultan's army was defeated on 17 December 1398, Timur's army killed and plundered in Delhi for three days and nights, leaving the city sacked, destroyed and in ruins. 100,000 war prisoners were said to have been put to death in one day. The Malwa, Gujarat, and Bahmani sultanates then rose, and the Bahmani sultanate split in 1518 into five Deccan sultanates.

The Chola Empire was a medieval thalassocratic empire based in southern India, with dominions and spheres of influence in southeast Asia. Its power showed in expeditions to the Ganges, naval raids on cities of the Srivijaya Empire on Sumatra, and repeated embassies to China.

The Vijayanagara Empire was established in 1336 by the brothers Harihara I and Bukka Raya I of the Sangama dynasty. It rose to prominence after the Delhi Sultanate's invasion of India, when the Hindu states of the Deccan were repeatedly raided and attacked, and four kingdoms had been conquered by 1317. After the neighbouring Kampili kingdom was defeated by the armies of the Delhi Sultanate, its populace committed a jauhar, a ritual mass suicide, in c. 1327–28.

Alauddin Khalji reigned for 20 years and conquered Rajputana, attacking and seizing Jaisalmer in 1299, Ranthambhor in 1301, Chittorgarh in 1303 and Malwa in 1305. He also conquered Gujarat, plundered the wealthy state of Devagiri, and withstood two Mongol raids. Under him the Delhi Sultanate reached its greatest territorial extent, but he was known for cruelty against the kingdoms he attacked. Historians note him as a tyrant: anyone he suspected of threatening his power was killed, along with the women and children of that family.

The Tughlaq dynasty came to power in 1320 when Ghazi Malik attacked Delhi and killed Khusro Khan, then took the throne as Ghiyath al-Din Tughluq. It reached its greatest extent through campaigns led by Muhammad bin Tughluq between 1330 and 1335. In 1398 Timur defeated four armies of the Sultanate; Delhi was plundered for eight days, its population massacred, and over 100,000 prisoners killed. The last Tughlaq sultan was eventually deposed by Khizr Khan, who founded the Sayyid dynasty.

Around 1118, the Cholas lost control of Vengi to the Western Chalukya and Gangavadi to the Hoysala Empire. After Vikrama Chola succeeded Kulothunga Chola I, the Cholas recovered both provinces. Chola power began declining after Kulothunga Chola III was defeated by Maravarman Sundara Pandiyan II in 1215 to 1216.

Commanders serving Alauddin Khalji collected war spoils from conquered kingdoms and paid khums, one fifth of the booty (ghanima) taken in war, into the Sultan's treasury. This helped strengthen Khalji rule as his generals, such as Malik Kafur and Khusraw Khan, expanded the Sultanate into South India, collecting large war booty from those they defeated. In 1308 Malik Kafur captured Warangal, raided Madurai and looted the treasuries of the capitals and the temples of south India, including the Warangal loot that held the Koh-i-Noor diamond. He returned to Delhi in 1311 laden with loot.

Muhammad bin Tughlaq sharply raised taxes on his ever-shrinking empire. Ibn Battuta noted that he paid his army, judges and officials by granting them the right to force collect taxes on Hindu villages, keep a portion and send the rest to the treasury. Those who failed to pay taxes were hunted and executed. He died in March 1351 while trying to chase and punish people in Sindh and Gujarat for rebellion and refusing to pay taxes.

In 1338 Muhammad bin Tughlaq's own nephew rebelled in Malwa; he attacked Malwa, caught the nephew and flayed him alive. By 1339, eastern regions under local Muslim governors and southern parts led by Hindu kings had revolted and declared independence from the Delhi Sultanate. By 1347 the Deccan had revolted under Ismail Mukh, an Afghan, who, elderly and with no interest in ruling, stepped down in favour of Zafar Khan, founder of the Bahmanid Sultanate.

In 1407, Firuz Bahmani of the Bahmani Sultanate made a treaty requiring Deva Raya I of Vijayanagara to pay an annual tribute of 100,000 huns, five maunds of pearls and fifty elephants. The Sultanate invaded in 1417 when Vijayanagara defaulted on the payment.

philosophy.text: Lingayatism is a distinct Shaivite tradition established in the 12th century by the philosopher and social reformer Basavanna. It remains especially influential in South India, particularly in the state of Karnataka.

Sikhism was founded in the 15th century in Northern India, based on the teachings of Guru Nanak and the nine successive Sikh Gurus. It arose during the early Islamic period, which the article dates from 1100 to 1500 CE. Most of its followers come from the Punjab region.

Lingayats take their name from the Kannada word Lingavantha, meaning one who wears the Ishtalinga on their body. The Ishtalinga is an oval-shaped emblem that symbolises Parasiva, the absolute reality.

Around 1374 to 1380, the Hindu philosopher Vidyaranya wrote the Sarva-darsana-samgraha, a compendium of all the philosophical systems. It included several Hindu systems beyond the six orthodox schools. He counted sixteen schools of Indian philosophy, adding those of the Saiva and Rasesvara traditions.

Historian Richard Eaton argues that the caste system in Bengal emerged into something resembling its modern form only between 1200 and 1500. He calls it far from the ancient and unchanging essence of Indian civilisation that generations of Orientalists supposed. Medieval Islamic Sultanates used social stratification to rule and collect tax revenue from non-Muslims.

Historian Peter Jackson says that speculative hypotheses blamed the caste system in Hindu states during the Delhi Sultanate period (about 1200 to 1500) for Hindu weakness in resisting the plunder by Islamic armies. He calls the idea appealing at first sight, but says it does not withstand closer scrutiny. Hindu warriors and soldiers of the period included Vaishyas and Shudras, not only Kshatriyas as the theoretical model says. He also finds no evidence of widespread conversion to Islam by lower-caste Hindus at the turn of the twelfth century.

Ram Sharan Sharma argued in his 1998 book Early Medieval Indian Society that dividing Indian history by eras of religious dominance misses the real causes of change. He saw the move to the middle ages as a shift toward rule based on land grants, responding to a crisis of state authority and caste adherence.

culture.text: Chaturanga was invented in medieval India and later exported to Europe, where it became chess. It is counted among the accomplishments of the period, alongside the scholarship of the Buddhist Nalanda mahavihara in modern-day Bihar.

From the medieval era onwards, influences from the Muslim world, particularly Central Asia and the Middle East, became prevalent in South Asian culture. The Delhi Sultanate, having conquered most of India by the 13th century, ushered in over five centuries of Indo-Muslim rule. It helped turn Delhi into a cosmopolitan and powerful hub in the Islamic world.

The Eastern Ganga dynasty ruled Kalinga from the 11th century to the early 15th century, and its rule saw a new style of temple architecture come into being. They are remembered as the builders of the Konark Sun Temple in Odisha, a World Heritage Site. It was built by King Narasimhadeva I (1238 to 1264 CE).

Slavery in India escalated during the Muslim conquests and domination of northern India from the 11th century. It became a social institution with the enslavement of Hindus, along with the use of slaves in armies, a practice within Muslim kingdoms of the time. According to Muslim historians of the Delhi Sultanate and the Mughal Empire era, after the invasions of Hindu kingdoms, other Indians were taken as slaves, with many exported to Central Asia and West Asia.

The Pala Empire on the Indo Gangetic Plain sponsored Buddhist institutions at the start of the medieval period, when Buddhism was predominant throughout the area. One such institution was Nalanda in modern-day Bihar, a centre of scholarship that brought a divided South Asia onto the global intellectual stage.

After Mahmud of Ghazni's twelfth expedition into India in 1018 to 1019, he is reported to have returned with so many slaves that their value fell to only two to ten dirhams each. Al-Utbi wrote that merchants came from distant cities to buy them, so that Central Asia, Iraq and Khurasan were swelled with them.

The Eastern Ganga kingdom prospered through trade and commerce, and its wealth was mostly used in the construction of temples. The dynasty's rule came to an end under King Bhanudeva IV (1414 to 1434 CE), in the early 15th century.

Slaves from the Horn of Africa were imported into the Indian subcontinent to serve in the households of the powerful or in the armies of the Deccan Sultanates. The Somali sultan Jamal ad-Din II (1424 to 1433) sent conquered Ethiopian captives to India. Ludovico di Varthema, who visited Zeila in 1503, described Abyssinian slaves captured in war being exported from the Somali coast to India.
